lesson_title: Two Drawings Beat a Memorised Table
hook_text: Six trig values, zero memorising. A road sign and a serviette are all you need.
clip_script: Shape one: an equilateral triangle — picture a triangular road sign — with all three sides two units and all three corners sixty degrees. Cut it straight down the middle from the top. The base halves into one and one; the top corner halves into thirty and thirty; the cut itself is the height. Pythagoras: two squared minus one squared is three, so the height is root three. Sit at the sixty-degree corner. Facing you: the cut, root three. Beside you: the half-base, one. The slant: two. So sine sixty is root three over two, cosine sixty is one half, tangent sixty is root three. Shape two: a square serviette of side one, folded corner to corner: a square corner, two forty-five-degree corners, and a diagonal of root two. Two shapes, six values, nothing memorised.
visual_style: A triangular road sign slicing cleanly in half with Pythagoras filling in root three, then a paper serviette folding on the diagonal, values popping off each side as they are read.
pacing: Deliberate on the cut, quick reads as the six values land, a beat of triumph on 'nothing memorised'.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and evaluate the special-angle expression without a calculator.
